digest.top_line: Dose-adapted single-isocenter SRS for 4 to 10 brain mets (prospective): 22/40 outlived DS-GPA prediction, 1-yr local failure 5%, no G3-5 toxicity.
digest.tldr: A CNS-only day on linac single-isocenter SRS for multiple brain mets. The one prospective cohort shows 1-yr local failure 5% with no G3-5 toxicity. Four planning or retrospective studies favor HyperArc and non-coplanar VMAT on gradient and V12Gy, and a simulated 1 mm GTV-PTV margin restored coverage lost to residual setup error.

sites.intro: All five studies address single-isocenter linac SRS technique. Only one is prospective, and the rest rely on dosimetric surrogates or retrospective local control.

studies.name: Manual to automated (HyperArc) VMAT SRS transition
studies.tldr: Paddick GI 5.42 vs 7.09 (P<.001), time in room 10.5 vs 11.4 min, RTOG CI unchanged; HyperArc 1-yr LC 90.1% across 377 mets.
details: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective: 693 single-isocenter VMAT SRS plans, HyperArc vs the prior 15 months of manual VMAT
🔍 HyperArc: 23-pt 2017 pilot + 350 pts over 15 months; mVMAT: 320 pts treated just before adoption
💊 GTV with no margin (PTV=GTV); 18-20 Gy x1, or 30 Gy/5 fx if any target >2-3 cm or deep
🔍 10 MV FFF on Edge with HD120 MLC; HyperArc used 2-4 arcs, Encompass open mask, 6DOF couch

details.text: 📊 HyperArc vs mVMAT: plan quality, QA and workflow (medians)
📐 Gradient gain holds at matched table-angle count
subdetails: 2 table angles (88 vs 261 plans): Paddick GI 3.68 vs 4.67, P<.001
4 table angles (66 vs 58 plans): Paddick GI 7.53 vs 9.58, P<.001

details: 📊 Clinical cohort (HyperArc only): 107 pts, 377 mets; 1-yr LC 90.1%, 47 tumors at risk
📊 Grade 3 seizures in 3 pts; no grade 4 or 5 events at median clinical f/u 7 mo
⚠️ Median imaging f/u 5 mo; 1-yr LC rests on 47 tumors at risk
⚠️ Different Eclipse versions (15.5 vs 13.6) confound technique vs software era
⚠️ Planning-time parity reflects 9 yrs of in-house mVMAT expertise; efficiency for novice planners is asserted, not measured
⚠️ Several authors report Varian grants, fees or patents

verdict.rationale: Retrospective historical-control dosimetric comparison; clinical outcomes single-arm HyperArc only with 5-mo median imaging f/u and toxicity scored by chart review.
verdict.audience: Brain metastases treated with single-isocenter linac SRS, no PTV margin

studies.significance: The gradient advantage is not just more arcs: at 2 table angles Paddick GI was 3.68 vs 4.67 (P<.001), and conformity was unchanged. Zero-margin single-isocenter multitarget delivery still gave 1-yr LC 90.1%, which supports keeping PTV=GTV when localization and intrafraction motion are tightly managed.
studies.monday_clinic: For multiple brain mets planned single-isocenter with PTV=GTV, this supports automated HyperArc as plan-quality parity with an expert manual VMAT program; it does not address targets far from isocenter, benign or vascular indications, or late radionecrosis.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Single-institution retrospective** comparison of 693 single-isocenter VMAT SRS plans: HyperArc (23-pt pilot + 350 pts) vs **320 consecutive prior mVMAT pts** as historical control. Clinical outcomes evaluated **only in the HyperArc cohort**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Plan cohort mixed metastatic and benign/vascular targets; 59.9% single-target, 12.0% with 6 to 22 targets. Clinical cohort: **107 pts with 377 brain mets**, median age 58, mostly NSCLC, breast and melanoma.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **No margin on GTV.** 18-20 Gy in 1 fx, or **30 Gy/5 fx** when any target exceeded 2-3 cm or involved deep structures. 10 MV FFF, HD120 MLC, CBCT with 6DOF correction.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Per-target conformity, gradient and falloff indices, mean brain dose, film PSQA against TG-218, planning and delivery times. Clinical: lesion-level LC (no 25% diameter increase) and grade 3+ CTCAE v5 toxicity.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Conformity equivalent; **gradient and falloff favor HyperArc**; mean brain dose 4.6% vs 5.1%. **1-yr LC 90.1%**, 3 grade 3 seizures, no grade 4/5.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Builds on the Clark 2012 class solution and the Thomas 2014 low-dose-spill penalty that matched Gamma Knife plans. Here the automated tool reaches that expert-solution level without nested tuning structures.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents single-isocenter linac SRS for brain mets with PTV=GTV at a center experienced in VMAT SRS. Does not represent benign or vascular targets, or a clinical head-to-head against manual VMAT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Software version differs between eras (Eclipse 15.5 vs 13.6). Planning time measured from structure-set timestamps as a surrogate. LC depends on 47 tumors at risk at 1 year.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case for automation is **standardization**, not a dosimetric leap: an expert manual program already sits near the ceiling. What remains unsettled is rotational-error underdosing of off-isocenter targets with zero margin, and which plan-quality metric actually tracks clinical outcome.

studies.interpretation:
The useful framing here is that the comparator is not average manual VMAT but a mature in-house class solution with nine years of planner experience behind it. Against that ceiling, an automated optimizer matched conformity (RTOG 1.14 vs 1.13) and improved gradient and falloff. That is a stronger statement than most planning comparisons, which pit a vendor tool against a handful of replanned cases, and it is the paper's main strength: 693 clinical plans pulled computationally from a DICOM-RT database rather than curated examples.

The gradient finding deserves the most attention because it is the one that could plausibly matter clinically, through low-dose spill and radionecrosis risk, and because it has an obvious confounder. HyperArc plans used more arcs (median 3 vs 2). The authors addressed this by stratifying on table-angle count, and the gradient advantage persisted at both 2 and 4 angles (3.68 vs 4.67 and 7.53 vs 9.58). That moves confidence toward a true optimizer effect, though the two eras also ran different Eclipse versions, so software generation and technique cannot be fully separated. The mean brain dose difference (4.6% vs 5.1%) is small and its distribution did not differ, so it should not be read as a dose-sparing result.

The clinical data are a different kind of evidence and should be weighted accordingly. LC of 90.1% at 1 year comes from a HyperArc-only cohort with median imaging follow-up of 5 months and 47 tumors at risk at the 1-year mark. There is no manual-VMAT clinical arm, so the paper cannot say automation changed outcomes; it can only say outcomes were not obviously compromised. The authors frame it as congruent with historical series, which is the right ceiling for this claim. Toxicity was scored retrospectively from chart review, and 7 months of clinical follow-up is too short to capture radionecrosis, which is the late effect a gradient improvement would be expected to influence.

The most practice-relevant methodological choice is zero PTV margin with a single isocenter for targets anywhere in the brain. The authors are candid that rotational misalignment could underdose distant targets and that other groups have added margin or split isocenters instead. The reported LC supports their approach under their IGRT conditions (6DOF couch, CBCT, short delivery), but the paper does not report LC by distance from isocenter, so it cannot settle that debate.

On efficiency, delivery and in-room time fell, while planning time did not. The claim that a less experienced planner would plan faster is plausible but untested here, since the planners were experts. Readers should also weigh that several authors report Varian financial relationships. Net: a credible demonstration that automated single-isocenter SRS reaches expert-level plan quality, with a clinical signal too immature to separate the technique from the institution.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Gradient improvement persists at matched table-angle counts (Paddick GI 3.68 vs 4.67 at 2 angles), so it reflects the optimizer, not arc number alone. Zero-margin single-isocenter delivery with 1-yr LC 90.1% supports PTV=GTV under tight IGRT, though off-isocenter rotational error remains unaddressed.

open_questions: Underdosing of off-isocenter targets from rotational error with zero margin
Which plan-quality metric predicts LC and radionecrosis
Durability of LC and late toxicity beyond 1 year

studies.name: Dose-adapted single-isocenter SRS for 4 to 10 brain mets (prospective)
studies.tldr: mOS 8.1 mo, 1-yr OS 35.7%; 22/40 outlived DS-GPA prediction (≥17 needed for non-inferiority), 1-yr local failure 5%, no G3-5 toxicity.
details: 🔍 Prospective single-arm, N=40, single institution (Durham, NC), accrued Feb 2017 to Aug 2019
🔍 1° EP OS, benchmarked against DS-GPA-predicted survival; non-inferiority if ≥17/40 outlived prediction
📊 22 pts outlived DS-GPA-predicted survival from protocol SRS, clearing the 17-pt threshold
📊 mOS 8.1 mo (5-12.1), 6-mo OS 57.3%, 1-yr OS 35.7%; median f/u 15.2 mo

details.text: 🔍 Dose-adapted SIMT algorithm (VMAT, 1 mm PTV margin)
subdetails: PTV >3 cm, any brainstem lesion, or V12Gy >20 mL: 5 Gy x5 to all lesions
Eloquent-area lesions could drop to 18 Gy or 16 Gy at MD discretion

details: 📊 1-yr local failure 5% (10 of 204 lesions) in 4 of 32 evaluable pts; 1 NSCLC pt had 5 of the failures
📊 Distant brain recurrence cumulative incidence 20% at 6 mo, 35.8% at 12 mo; 19 of 40 pts
📊 AEs in 73%, all G1-2 (headache 50%, fatigue 45%); no G3-5 treatment-related AEs
📐 Median beam-on 8 min; median brain V12Gy 11.7 mL (1fx), V24Gy 3.5 mL (5fx); median hippocampal dose 2.4 Gy
⚠️ 8 of 40 pts died before first MRI, so LC/DBF denominators are 32 pts
⚠️ 11 pts had prior SRS/WBRT; neurocognitive testing attrition steep after 6 mo
⚠️ Discussion cites 58% 6-mo distant failure, contradicting the 20% 6-mo cumulative incidence in Results
⚠️ Varian-funded; PIs report Varian funding directly related to the study

verdict.rationale: Single-arm, N=40, single institution; OS benchmarked against a DS-GPA prediction, not a randomized WBRT or multi-isocenter comparator. Too few events for LC or necrosis modeling.
verdict.audience: 4-10 untreated brain mets, KPS ≥70, excluding SCLC, lymphoma, germ-cell, LMD

studies.significance: The transferable piece is the dose-adaptation rule: switching every lesion to 5 Gy x5 when V12Gy exceeds 20 mL or a brainstem lesion is present gave 98% per-lesion LC with 1.3% necrosis, at aggregate PTV up to 32 mL. That supports hypofractionating the whole plan in high-volume cases instead of de-escalating single-fraction dose.
studies.monday_clinic: For a KPS ≥70 pt with 4 to 10 non-SCLC brain mets and aggregate volume pushing single-fraction V12Gy past 20 mL, this supports a single-isocenter 5 Gy x5 plan as a feasible SRS option; it does not address SCLC, leptomeningeal disease, or more than 10 lesions.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective **single-arm** trial, **N=40**, enrolled Feb 2017 to Aug 2019, registered NCT02886572. Median follow-up **15.2 mo**. Funded by Varian Medical Systems.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **4 to 10 untreated brain mets**, age ≥18, **KPS ≥70**, life expectancy >3 mo, DS-GPA ≥0.5, largest lesion ≤4 cm, >2 mm from optic apparatus; brainstem lesions allowed. Excluded SCLC, germ-cell, lymphoma, leukemia, myeloma, leptomeningeal disease. Median age 61, KPS 90, 6 mets; NSCLC 50%, breast 27.5%; 11 had prior SRS/WBRT.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Single-isocenter VMAT, 1 mm PTV margin. **20 Gy** for PTV <2 cm, **18 Gy** for 2.0 to <3.0 cm; **5 Gy x5 to all lesions** if any PTV >3 cm, any brainstem lesion, or brain V12Gy >20 mL. 24 pts (125 lesions) got 1 fraction, 16 pts (79 lesions) got 5; median beam-on 8 min.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: OS**, judged non-inferior if ≥17 of 40 pts outlived DS-GPA-predicted survival. Secondary: local recurrence, distant brain recurrence, neurologic death, AEs, QOL, steroid use.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **22 pts outlived prediction**; mOS **8.1 mo**, 1-yr OS **35.7%**. 1-yr local failure **5%** (10 of 204 lesions); distant brain recurrence **35.8%** at 12 mo. Neurologic death 20% of deaths.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: AEs in 73%, **all G1-2**, mostly headache and fatigue; **no G3-5 treatment-related AEs**. Radionecrosis in 5 lesions in 4 pts; 2 pts needed surgery. MMSE, Trail Making, HVLT and FACT-Br unchanged at 3 mo.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: mOS of 8.1 mo sits inside the range of prior multi-met SRS series summarized in the paper's Table 4 (medians 5.8 to 14.1 mo), most of them retrospective. The randomized SRS vs WBRT trials for 4 to 20 mets (NCT03550391, NCT03075072, NCT01592968) are the comparators this cannot replace.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents KPS ≥70 pts with 4 to 10 non-SCLC brain mets, lesions ≤4 cm, treated on a linac SIMT platform. Does not represent SCLC, leptomeningeal disease, >10 lesions, or pts expected to live <3 mo.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The DS-GPA benchmark uses the original formulation, measures from first brain-met diagnosis, and was applied here from protocol SRS in a cohort where 11 had prior brain RT. LC and DBF exclude the 8 pts who died before first MRI, and the paper's own Discussion gives a 6-mo distant failure figure (58%) that conflicts with its Results (20%).

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The OS endpoint mostly shows the technique does not shorten life against a prognostic index; it cannot show SRS beats WBRT. The more usable signal is the per-lesion one: 5-fraction plans held **98% LC** with low necrosis despite larger volumes, which supports hypofractionating high-volume multi-met plans.

studies.interpretation:
This trial asks a narrower question than its title suggests. Its primary endpoint is not whether single-isocenter SRS controls disease better than whole-brain RT, but whether treating 4 to 10 metastases this way shortens survival compared with what a prognostic index predicts. Clearing the bar (22 pts outlived their DS-GPA estimate against a threshold of 17) tells a reader the technique does not appear to cost survival in a selected, KPS-90 cohort. It does not tell them SRS is preferable to WBRT for this number of lesions. That question belongs to the randomized trials the authors name (NCT03550391, NCT03075072, NCT01592968), and this paper should be read as feasibility and safety groundwork alongside them.

The benchmark itself deserves skepticism. The original DS-GPA estimates survival from first diagnosis of brain metastases, while the primary analysis here starts the clock at protocol SRS, and 11 of 40 pts had already received brain RT. Measuring from a later time point biases toward shorter observed survival, so the comparison is probably conservative for the technique. On the other hand, the cohort was screened for life expectancy over 3 months, DS-GPA of at least 0.5 and KPS of at least 70, so the people enrolled were already the ones most likely to beat a population-level estimate. Those two biases pull in opposite directions, and with 40 pts there is no way to net them out.

The RT-relevant content sits in the dose-adaptation rule and the per-lesion outcomes. Rather than reducing single-fraction dose to fit a crowded plan, the protocol moved every lesion to 5 Gy x5 once any lesion exceeded 3 cm, any lesion sat in the brainstem, or brain V12Gy passed 20 mL. Those 5-fraction plans lost 2 of 79 lesions locally against 8 of 119 for unadjusted single-fraction lesions, with necrosis of 1.3% versus 3.4%. The groups are not randomized and differ by design (the 5-fraction group carried the larger volumes), so the contrast cannot be read as fractionation causing better control. What it does support is that hypofractionation absorbed the high-volume cases without an obvious penalty in control or necrosis, at aggregate PTVs up to 32 mL. That speaks directly to the Alliance question in resected cavities the authors cite and to the unanswered intact-lesion version of it.

Several reporting issues lower confidence in the secondary numbers. The local and distant failure analyses include only the 32 pts who reached a first MRI, so the 8 earliest deaths are not counted in the denominator. The Discussion quotes a 6-month distant failure risk of 58%, which cannot be reconciled with the 20% cumulative incidence at 6 months in Results. Lesion counts by fractionation (119 plus 79) do not sum to the 204 treated lesions. None of these overturns the main message, but together they suggest the secondary endpoints are descriptive, which the authors acknowledge when they note too few events for time-to-event modeling of local failure or necrosis.

The neurocognitive and QOL stability at 3 months is reassuring and fits the low hippocampal and integral brain doses reported, but testing attrition after 6 months, driven largely by death, means these data cannot speak to the late decline that defines the WBRT trade-off. For practice, the study supports single-isocenter, volume-adapted SRS as a workable option for 4 to 10 lesions in fit pts, and the V12Gy-triggered switch to 5 fractions as a planning rule worth adopting. It leaves the comparative question to the randomized trials.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The transferable piece is the dose-adaptation rule: switching every lesion to 5 Gy x5 when V12Gy exceeds 20 mL or a brainstem lesion is present gave 98% per-lesion LC with 1.3% necrosis, at aggregate PTV up to 32 mL. That supports hypofractionating the whole plan in high-volume cases instead of de-escalating single-fraction dose.

studies.name: Interinstitutional plan quality: Elements MME vs RapidArc single-isocenter SRS
studies.tldr: RapidArc lowered median V12Gy 19.2 vs 23.7 cc (P<.0001) and improved conformity; MME lowered V5Gy and mean brain dose (2.57 vs 2.76 Gy).
details: 🔍 Paired replanning study: 30 pts, 4-10 brain mets (217 targets), each planned on both platforms
🔍 Each institution replanned the other's 15 cases with its own expert technique (TJU = MME, UAB = RA)

subdetails: RA (VMAT): 2-4 noncoplanar arcs, 10 MV FFF, Eclipse 13.6, AAA dose calc
MME (DCA): 4-9 noncoplanar DCAs, 6 MV FFF, Elements v1.5, pencil-beam dose calc
Both: single isocenter, HD120 MLC, 14-24 Gy single fraction, D99% = 100% Rx goal
All 60 plans exported to MIM for DVH analysis, removing inter-TPS calculation bias

details.text: 📊 Dosimetric medians, MME vs RA (paired Wilcoxon)

details: 📊 RA gave lower V12Gy in 26 of 30 cases; MME gave lower V5Gy in 25 of 30
📊 Total PTV <2.1 cc (6 cases): MME favorable for V8, V5, Dmean; V12 favored MME in 4 of 6
📊 Total PTV >2.1 cc (24 cases): V12 favored RA, Element/VMAT ratio mean 1.24
📐 Brain DVHs cross near 6 Gy (6.8 Gy in representative case): RA better above, MME better below
📐 Table 1 means widen the low-dose gap: V5Gy 158.3 vs 174.8 cc, Dmean 2.66 vs 3.03 Gy
🔍 Estimated beam-on: MME ~6-9 min at 6 MV FFF; RA 3-4 min at 10 MV FFF
⚠️ Beam energy confound: 6 MV FFF (MME) vs 10 MV FFF (RA), by commissioning, not design
⚠️ Dosimetric surrogates only; no toxicity, radionecrosis, or cognitive outcomes
⚠️ Internal inconsistencies: V12 MME median 23.7 in text vs 24.0 in Table 1; RA RTOG CI 1.21 vs 1.23
⚠️ Software versions dated (Eclipse 13.6, MME 1.5); HyperArc not tested
⚠️ Several UAB authors report Varian research support or consulting

verdict.rationale: Dosimetric planning study with no clinical endpoints; 6 vs 10 MV energy and two dose algorithms confound the platform comparison. Platform and planner effects not separable.
verdict.audience: 4-10 brain metastases, single-isocenter linac SRS, single fraction

studies.significance: The platforms trade dose bands rather than one beating the other. RA lowers the V12Gy/V8Gy band tied to radionecrosis, while MME lowers dose below roughly 6 Gy. The V12 advantage holds only above 2.1 cc total PTV (ratio mean 1.24); below that, MME matched or beat RA on V12 in 4 of 6 cases.
studies.monday_clinic: For a pt with 4-10 brain mets and total PTV above 2.1 cc, this favors single-isocenter VMAT for lower V12Gy. With very small total PTV, MME matched or beat RA on V12 in 4 of 6 cases. Low-dose spill differences have no outcome correlation yet.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Paired dosimetric **replanning study** at 2 institutions (TJU, UAB). 15 previously treated pts from each site were replanned by the other site with its own technique. Comparison by **paired 2-tailed Wilcoxon signed-rank**, prespecified α .05.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **30 pts with 4 to 10 brain metastases**, 217 targets, median 7.5 per case. Individual target volume 0.014 to 17.73 cm3; total PTV 0.49 to 27.32 cm3, median 7.05 cm3.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **14 to 24 Gy single fraction**, prescriptions unchanged between plans and largely RTOG 9508-based. RA used 2 to 4 noncoplanar VMAT arcs at 10 MV FFF with 3 ring tuning structures. MME used automated noncoplanar DCAs at 6 MV FFF with up to 1 mm MLC margin and island-blocking avoidance.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Per target: RTOG CI, Paddick CI, coverage. Per plan: **V12Gy, V8Gy, V5Gy, mean brain dose**, plus arc, MU, and beam-on estimates.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: RA favored conformity and the **V12Gy/V8Gy** band; MME favored **V5Gy and Dmean**. The brain DVHs cross near **6 Gy**, and below 2.1 cc total PTV MME was favorable on most metrics.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Gevaert et al (10 cases, 40 mets) found higher V12Gy and V5Gy for RA. Its Paddick CI of 0.65 ± 0.08 (MME) and 0.67 ± 0.16 (RA) sits below this study's 0.70 and 0.77, which the authors read as plans that were not fully optimized. Narayanasamy et al (8 pts, 40 targets) found the platforms comparable but was likely underpowered.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents 4 to 10 brain mets planned by expert single-isocenter linac teams on Eclipse 13.6 RA or Elements MME v1.5. Does not represent HyperArc, newer MME versions, >10 targets, fractionated SRS, or less experienced VMAT planners.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: **Different beam energies and dose algorithms** (pencil beam vs AAA) per platform, so platform effects cannot be cleanly separated from energy and algorithm. Each platform had one expert institution, so planner skill is part of the RA result. Hotspots and homogeneity were not compared, and text and Table 1 medians disagree for V12.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Both platforms met clinical goals, and the differences are small and dose-band specific. Moderate isodose spill has retrospective links to radionecrosis, while low-dose spill has **no toxicity correlation yet**. It may matter more as pts survive to repeat SRS or WBRT.

studies.interpretation:
The useful frame for this comparison is that neither platform dominates; each wins a different part of the dose-volume curve, and the crossover sits near 6 Gy. That matters because the two bands carry very different levels of evidence. The moderate isodose region (V8 to V12) has a retrospective literature linking it to radionecrosis, so RA's lower V12Gy is the more clinically interpretable advantage. MME's edge sits in the low-dose bath, where the authors themselves acknowledge no toxicity correlation exists. The case for caring about low-dose spill rests on an argument about cumulative dose in long survivors receiving serial salvage courses, which is plausible but untested.

Against the two earlier head-to-head comparisons, this one is larger and better powered, and it reverses part of the Gevaert finding that RA also carried more low-dose spill. The authors attribute the earlier results to plans that were not fully optimized. That claim is supported by the Paddick CI gap, but it also reveals the central methodological problem: the result for VMAT depends heavily on who builds the plan. Every RA plan here came from one expert planner using the institution's own published technique. The RA arm is therefore closer to a best-case benchmark than to a typical community VMAT plan, while MME's automated templates are likely more reproducible across centers. A reader at a center without that VMAT expertise should expect RA's conformity and V12 advantage to shrink.

The second issue is confounding by hardware. MME ran at 6 MV FFF with a pencil-beam calculation, and RA ran at 10 MV FFF with AAA. Exporting all plans to MIM removes DVH-calculation differences, but it cannot remove differences already in each system's dose calculation, especially for very small targets near the field edge. The authors suggest penumbra shape may explain part of MME's low-dose advantage in small-volume cases. That means the volume-dependent finding, where MME is favorable when total PTV is under 2.1 cc, rests on 6 cases and is the result most exposed to this confound.

The effect sizes also deserve scrutiny before they drive platform decisions. The V5Gy medians differ by about a cubic centimetre despite P=.009, while the Table 1 means show a wider gap, so the distribution is skewed and a few cases drive the difference. Reporting discrepancies between the abstract, text, and table (RA RTOG CI 1.21 vs 1.23; MME V12 median 23.7 vs 24.0) do not change the direction but do lower confidence in the exact values.

What this does not settle is whether any of these differences changes outcomes. A prospective cohort linking platform-specific V12 and low-dose volumes to radionecrosis and neurocognition would. So would a replication with modern optimizers (HyperArc, newer Elements) using the shared de-identified dataset the authors offer. Until then, the reasonable reading is that both platforms are adequate. Expert VMAT buys a modest reduction in V12, and automated DCA buys consistency and a lower low-dose bath.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The platforms trade dose bands rather than one beating the other. RA lowers the V12Gy/V8Gy band tied to radionecrosis, while MME lowers dose below roughly 6 Gy. The V12 advantage holds only above 2.1 cc total PTV (ratio mean 1.24); below that, MME matched or beat RA on V12 in 4 of 6 cases.

open_questions: Does low-dose brain spill predict cognitive decline after repeat SRS?
Does HyperArc or newer Elements shift the dosimetric tradeoff?
How does non-expert VMAT planning compare with automated MME?

studies.name: Automated single-isocenter SRS for multiple brain mets: outcomes and margins
studies.tldr: 1y LC 89% per pt and 94% per lesion. Residual setup error caused coverage loss (V95 <95%) in 28 targets; simulated 1 mm GTV-PTV margin restored coverage.
details: 🔍 Retrospective, 2 Italian centers, 31 consecutive pts, 204 BM <3 cm, 4-10 BM per pt, Oct 2016-Sep 2018
🔍 Frameless mask, Brainlab Elements Multiple Brain Mets (automated DCA planning), single isocenter, ExacTrac 6D IGRT

subdetails: 20-22 Gy single fx for lesions <2 cm; 16-18 Gy for ≥2 cm or near brainstem/chiasm
Median CI 1.32, GI 3.94; median distance from isocenter 39 mm
Setup tolerance 0.5 mm / 0.5°; mean 3D residual error 0.34 mm (range 0.1-0.53)

details: 📊 mOS 16.1 mo; median time to distant brain failure 8 mo; salvage SRS in 15 pts, WBRT in 3
📊 No G3-4 toxicity. Radiologic necrosis in 5 (16.1%) pts; per-lesion risk 11% at 12 mo
📐 Individual V12Gy >10 cm3 predicted necrosis (P=.01); lesion number and cumulative volume did not

details.text: 📊 Coverage loss (V95 <95%) from residual isocenter error, 28 targets

details: 📊 Simulated 0 mm margin: coverage compromised in 18 lesions; 1 mm margin: adequate coverage in all lesions
📊 Intrafraction: 10 positionings in 7 (22%) pts out of tolerance; uncorrected → GTV coverage loss in 21 (28%) of 74 lesions
📊 1 mm margin held GTV coverage under intrafraction drift in all but 2 lesions

details.text: 📐 Volume cost of margin, spherical lesion (Table 4)

details: 🔗 Roper et al: 0.5° simulated rotation spared coverage; up to 2° lost coverage in more than one-third of cases
🔗 Korytko et al: V12Gy >10 cm3 necrosis risk 55.3% vs 22.5% below, in 198 GK-treated tumors
⚠️ Margin sufficiency is dosimetric (CBCT re-computation), not linked to per-lesion LC by margin size
⚠️ Internal inconsistency: abstract says 14 pts with 4-6 and 17 with 7-10 BM; Table 1 says 20 with 4-7, 11 with 8-10
⚠️ Coverage-loss pts reported as 10 (abstract) vs 12 (results); intrafraction section says 1 mm held all but 2 lesions
⚠️ No formal neurocognitive testing; only 9 pts on concurrent systemic therapy, limiting IO/TKI-era transfer

verdict.rationale: Retrospective 31-pt series, median f/u 11 mo, no comparator arm; margin conclusion rests on dosimetric re-computation, not lesion-level clinical failure by margin.
verdict.audience: 4-10 brain mets <3 cm, frameless linac SRS, lung/breast/melanoma-dominant

studies.significance: Coverage loss clustered in small lesions far from isocenter: about 90% of V95 <95% misses were lesions <0.4 cm3 at ≥3.9 cm. Uncorrected intrafraction drift cost GTV coverage in 28% of lesions, so the 1 mm margin depends on 6D monitoring with mid-treatment correction.
studies.monday_clinic: For a pt with 4-10 small brain mets on a frameless linac with 6D ExacTrac and mid-treatment re-imaging, this supports a 1 mm GTV-PTV margin over 0 mm; it does not address mask setups without intrafraction correction or cumulative volumes ≥15 cm3.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Retrospective** two-center series (Rome, Negrar), 31 consecutive pts, 204 BM. Outcomes by Kaplan-Meier from SRS; dosimetric accuracy from offline CBCT fused to planning CT with residual shifts applied.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Age ≥18, **4-10 BM <3 cm**. Median age 60; lung 14, melanoma 8, breast 5. Concurrent systemic therapy in 9 pts (IO 4, targeted 5).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Single-isocenter DCA via Brainlab Elements, 10 noncoplanar arcs at 5 couch positions. **20-22 Gy** for <2 cm, **16-18 Gy** for ≥2 cm or near critical structures; PTV = GTV + **1 mm** (176 lesions) or 2 mm (28).

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: 1y/2y LC **89%/77%** per pt, **94%/86%** per lesion; mOS 16.1 mo. Coverage loss (V95 <95%) in 28 targets, driven by distance ≥39 mm (P=.0001) and volume <0.40 cm3 (P=.015).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No G3-4** toxicity. Necrosis in 5 (16.1%) pts, 11% per lesion at 12 mo, 2 with G2 motor deficit; individual **V12Gy >10 cm3** predicted it (P=.01).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Roper et al showed coverage held at 0.5° simulated rotation but failed in over one-third of plans at 2°; here measured residuals stayed within 0.5 mm / 0.5° tolerance, which is why 1 mm sufficed. Necrosis tracking V12Gy matches the Korytko gamma knife series the authors cite.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents 4-10 small BM treated frameless on a linac with 6D setup and intrafraction correction. Does not represent setups without mid-treatment imaging, lesions ≥3 cm, or pts needing formal neurocognitive endpoints.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The paper reports pt counts inconsistently (4-6/7-10 vs 4-7/8-10; 10 vs 12 pts with coverage loss). LC is not stratified by margin or by distance from isocenter, so the clinical consequence of the dosimetric miss is untested.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The case for 1 mm is a trade-off: the margin rescues small distal targets while Table 4 shows each added millimetre inflates a 1 cm lesion's volume steeply, feeding V12Gy. That trade-off only holds if intrafraction drift is caught and corrected.

studies.interpretation:
The question this paper answers is narrower than its title suggests. Its clinical outcomes, 89% per-patient and 94% per-lesion local control at one year with no grade 3-4 toxicity, are what one would expect from any competent single-fraction SRS series at 20-22 Gy and add little on their own: 31 patients, a median follow-up of 11 months, no comparator, and survival driven by extracranial control and concurrent systemic therapy. The contribution is the geometric one, and it addresses a specific worry about single-isocenter multi-target treatment: a rotational error at the shared isocenter becomes a translational miss at a distant target, and the miss grows with distance.

Roper et al had framed the problem in simulation, with coverage holding at 0.5° but failing in more than a third of plans at 2°. This series supplies the missing piece, the residual errors actually delivered on a frameless mask with 6D ExacTrac correction. Mean 3D residual was 0.34 mm, and with errors that small the losses concentrated where geometry predicts, in lesions under 0.4 cm3 sitting at or beyond 3.9 cm from isocenter. A 1 mm margin absorbed them in re-computation. The read for a linac SRS program is that the margin decision depends on the error budget your own system achieves, and this paper gives one measured budget rather than a universal answer.

The intrafraction data carry the more practical warning. Ten positionings in 7 patients drifted out of tolerance, and left uncorrected that drift cost GTV coverage in 28% of the 74 lesions involved; even with 1 mm, 2 lesions stayed short. So the 1 mm conclusion is conditional on mid-treatment imaging and correction. A department running mask-based single-isocenter plans without intrafraction monitoring cannot borrow it.

The skeptic's case rests on three points. First, adequacy is defined dosimetrically, by V95 on a CBCT-fused re-computation, and the paper never links coverage loss or margin size to lesion-level failure; 11 lesions recurred, and we are not told whether they were the distal small targets. Second, the reporting is internally inconsistent on patient counts by lesion number and on how many patients had coverage loss, which lowers confidence in the denominator behind the subgroup statistics. Third, the 28 lesions planned with 2 mm are folded into the outcomes, so the clinical series is not a clean 1 mm cohort.

The margin's cost side is the stronger argument. The authors' own volume table shows how quickly an isotropic expansion inflates a small sphere, and necrosis here tracked individual V12Gy above 10 cm3 rather than lesion count or cumulative volume, in line with the Korytko gamma knife experience they cite. That points toward the smallest margin that holds coverage, not toward the 2-3 mm some early single-isocenter planning studies suggested. What would overturn the conclusion is a series with lesion-level local failure mapped against distance and margin showing excess misses in distal small targets at 1 mm, or a center whose residual errors run materially above the 0.5 mm / 0.5° tolerance used here. Until then this is a reasonable, system-specific justification for 1 mm, not evidence that the technique matches per-lesion isocenter SRS on control.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Coverage loss clustered in small lesions far from isocenter: about 90% of V95 <95% misses were lesions <0.4 cm3 at ≥3.9 cm. Uncorrected intrafraction drift cost GTV coverage in 28% of lesions, so the 1 mm margin depends on 6D monitoring with mid-treatment correction.

studies.name: DCAT vs CoVMAT vs NcVMAT for single brain met
studies.tldr: Non-coplanar VMAT cut normal-brain V12Gy to 9.4 vs 11.6 (DCAT) vs 15.1 cm3 (coplanar VMAT) for 2-3 cm single brain mets, 20 Gy/1 fx.
details: 🔍 Planning study: DCAT, CoVMAT and NcVMAT plans built for each of 15 pts, single institution (Kyoto)
🔍 Single brain met, longest diameter 2-3 cm; median PTV 6.4 cm3 (range 3.7-16.2)

subdetails: 20 Gy/1 fx to PTV, normalized to D99.5%
6 MV, TrueBeam STx, Eclipse 15.6 AcurosXB, 1 mm grid
PTV D2% set at ~142% of Rx (PTV covered by 70% isodose line)
DCAT and NcVMAT: 1 coplanar + 2 non-coplanar arcs; CoVMAT: 1 coplanar arc

details: 📊 RTOG-CI and Paddick CI significantly better with NcVMAT than DCAT
📊 GTV D98% better with NcVMAT than DCAT or CoVMAT
📊 Coplanar-only VMAT was worst on low-dose spill: V5Gy nearly doubled vs DCAT
📊 MU higher for DCAT and NcVMAT than CoVMAT; beam-on time longer for both VMAT plans than DCAT
⚠️ Dosimetric surrogate only: no radionecrosis, local control or neurocognitive outcomes
⚠️ Single TPS and optimizer; gains may depend on planner skill and Eclipse-specific tools (ring contour, NTO)
🔗 Molinier et al. is the only prior direct DCAT/CoVMAT/NcVMAT comparison, but used different TPS and algorithms between techniques

verdict.rationale: Planning study in 15 pts; dosimetric V12Gy surrogate stands in for radionecrosis, with no clinical outcomes, single TPS and single institution.
verdict.audience: Single brain met, 2-3 cm, LINAC SRS 20 Gy/1 fx

studies.significance: The coplanar-only VMAT many centers default to was the worst plan for low and intermediate spill (V12Gy 15.1 cm3, V5Gy 96.8 cm3), not merely a wash vs DCAT. For 2-3 cm lesions, where necrosis risk rises, adding non-coplanar arcs is what earns VMAT its advantage, at the cost of longer beam-on time.
studies.monday_clinic: In a 2-3 cm single brain met planned for LINAC SRS, this supports non-coplanar over coplanar-only VMAT when normal-brain V12Gy is the constraint; it does not address multiple mets, single-isocenter multi-target plans, or fractionated SRT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Dosimetric **planning study**: three plans (DCAT, CoVMAT, NcVMAT) per pt for **15 pts** treated April 2016 to October 2017, single institution. Two-way ANOVA with Bonferroni post-hoc for PTV/GTV indices; repeated-measures ANOVA with Holm for normal brain.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Single brain metastasis, longest diameter 2-3 cm**, chosen because local control and radionecrosis are worse than for smaller lesions. Median PTV 6.4 cm3 (range 3.7-16.2).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **20 Gy/1 fx** to PTV (GTV + 1 mm), normalized to D99.5%, 6 MV on TrueBeam STx, AcurosXB. PTV D2% held near 142% of Rx across techniques so the comparison is at matched heterogeneity.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: NcVMAT gave the **best conformity** (RTOG-CI and Paddick CI vs DCAT) and **lowest normal-brain V20 to V5Gy** vs both comparators. CoVMAT had the largest V15Gy through V5Gy and the fewest MU; both VMAT techniques ran longer beam-on than DCAT.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Vogelbaum et al. showed higher local recurrence and radionecrosis for mets >2.0 cm, which is the population chosen here. Molinier et al. compared the same three techniques but across mixed intracranial targets and with different TPS and algorithms, which this study removes as a confounder.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents LINAC SRS planning for a single 2-3 cm brain met at 20 Gy/1 fx on an Eclipse/TrueBeam platform. Does not represent multiple mets, Gamma Knife, fractionated SRT, or other planning systems.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: V12Gy is a planning surrogate for necrosis; no clinical outcomes were measured. Plan quality for inverse-optimized techniques is operator- and optimizer-dependent, and DCAT plans used manual MLC shaping, so the margin between techniques may not transfer across centers.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The useful finding is that coplanar-only VMAT is not an adequate substitute for non-coplanar DCAT on low-dose spill, while non-coplanar VMAT beats both. The cost is beam-on time, relevant for intrafraction motion in frameless SRS.

studies.interpretation:
The practical question this planning study speaks to is not whether VMAT beats DCAT in general, but whether the convenience of a single coplanar VMAT arc gives up anything for a mid-sized brain metastasis. On that point the data are fairly clear. Coplanar-only VMAT produced the largest normal-brain volumes at every level from 15 Gy down to 5 Gy, with V12Gy of 15.1 cm3 against 11.6 cm3 for DCAT and 9.4 cm3 for non-coplanar VMAT. The low-dose bath was the most striking divergence, with V5Gy of 96.8 cm3 for the coplanar plan against 49.2 and 42.9 cm3 for the two non-coplanar techniques. In other words, the arc geometry mattered more than the modulation: modulation layered onto non-coplanar arcs bought a further improvement, but modulation on a single coplanar arc was a step backward from conventional conformal arcs.

The population was chosen deliberately. Lesions of 2 to 3 cm sit in the zone where Vogelbaum and colleagues reported higher rates of local recurrence and radionecrosis than for lesions of 2 cm or less, so this is where a reduction in V12Gy has the most plausible clinical leverage. The authors lean on V12Gy as a radionecrosis predictor, which is a reasonable working assumption but remains an inference here: no patient in this comparison was treated three ways, and no toxicity or control endpoint was measured. The magnitude of the V12Gy difference between NcVMAT and DCAT is also modest relative to the spread within each arm, as the standard deviations show, so a reader should expect the benefit to vary considerably across individual lesions and to matter most for the larger and less spherical ones.

The design has one real strength over the prior comparison by Molinier and colleagues: all three techniques were planned in the same TPS with the same dose algorithm, normalization and target heterogeneity, so differences reflect technique rather than software. The flip side is that this is a single-center Eclipse experience, with inverse plans shaped by a ring contour and normal-tissue objective, and DCAT plans shaped by manual MLC adjustment. Inverse-optimized plan quality is notoriously dependent on planner and optimizer, so the size of the NcVMAT advantage may shrink or grow elsewhere. The study also does not address single-isocenter multi-target planning, which is where many centers now use VMAT most, or fractionated stereotactic RT, which is commonly chosen for lesions in this size range.

The trade-off a clinic must weigh is time. Both VMAT techniques had longer beam-on times than DCAT, and non-coplanar delivery adds couch rotations. In frameless mask-based SRS, longer treatment raises intrafraction motion risk against a 1 mm PTV margin, which could erode some of the dosimetric gain in practice. For a center already delivering non-coplanar arcs, the findings support moving those arcs to VMAT optimization when normal-brain dose is binding, such as a larger lesion or a pt likely to need repeat SRS. For a center delivering single coplanar VMAT arcs to solitary lesions, the data argue that the plan should at least be checked against a non-coplanar alternative.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The coplanar-only VMAT many centers default to was the worst plan for low and intermediate spill (V12Gy 15.1 cm3, V5Gy 96.8 cm3), not merely a wash vs DCAT. For 2-3 cm lesions, where necrosis risk rises, adding non-coplanar arcs is what earns VMAT its advantage, at the cost of longer beam-on time.

open_questions: Does lower planned V12Gy with NcVMAT reduce clinical radionecrosis?
Does the advantage hold for multiple mets or single-isocenter plans?
Does longer beam-on time erode the gain in frameless SRS?

papers.title: Transition From Manual to Automated Planning and Delivery of Volumetric Modulated Arc Therapy Stereotactic Radiosurgery: Clinical, Dosimetric, and Quality Assurance Results
Interinstitutional Plan Quality Assessment of 2 Linac-Based, Single-Isocenter, Multiple Metastasis Radiosurgery Techniques
Outcomes in Patients With 4 to 10 Brain Metastases Treated With Dose-Adapted Single-Isocenter Multitarget Stereotactic Radiosurgery: A Prospective Study
Initial Experience With Single-Isocenter Radiosurgery to Target Multiple Brain Metastases Using an Automated Treatment Planning Software: Clinical Outcomes and Optimal Target Volume Margins Strategy
Dosimetric comparison among dynamic conformal arc therapy, coplanar and non-coplanar volumetric modulated arc therapy for single brain metastasis
papers.abstract: Abstract In the delivery of stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) by linear accelerator (LINAC), dynamic conformal arc therapy (DCAT) with non-coplanar beams is conventionally used. However, volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) can improve target conformity, thereby decreasing the dose to organs at risk by inversed planning methods, but few studies have directly compared DCAT and VMAT with and without non-coplanar beams in patients with single brain metastasis. We therefore conducted a planning study to compare the dose distribution in DCAT, VMAT using only a coplanar arc (CoVMAT) and VMAT with non-coplanar arcs (NcVMAT) in the treatment of single brain metastasis. DCAT, CoVMAT and NcVMAT plans were created for 15 patients. The three modalities were compared in terms of target conformity, target coverage, the dose to normal brain tissue, monitor units (MUs) and beam-on time. Both conformity indices (RTOG-CI and IP-CI) as well as the D98% of the gross target volume (GTV) were significantly better in the NcVMAT plans than in the DCAT plans. Comparisons of the doses to normal brain tissue revealed that the V20Gy, V15Gy, V12Gy, V10Gy and V5Gy were significantly smaller in the NcVMAT plans than in the plans based on the other two modalities. The MUs of the DCAT and NcVMAT plans were larger than those of the CoVMAT plans, and the beam-on time was longer in the NcVMAT and CoVMAT plans than in the DCAT plans. Compared to the CoVMAT and DCAT plans, NcVMAT plans significantly improved target conformity and reduced the doses to normal brain tissue at V20Gy, V15Gy, V12Gy, V10Gy and V5Gy.
